snippet.title: Philip II: Alexander's Father Who Conquered All Greece
snippet.description:
Before Alexander the Great conquered the world, his father conquered Greece. In this short, we explore the rise of Philip II of Macedon, the brilliant king who transformed Macedonia from a vulnerable kingdom into the most powerful state in the Greek world. Through military reform, political skill, and relentless ambition, Philip changed history forever.

Philip II revolutionized warfare by creating the feared Macedonian phalanx, armed with the long sarissa spear, and by building a disciplined, professional army unlike anything Greece had seen before. But his victories were not won by force alone. Philip used diplomacy, marriages, alliances, and strategy to outmaneuver rival Greek city-states and expand Macedonian power step by step.

His greatest triumph came after the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, where Philip decisively defeated the combined forces of Athens and Thebes. That victory made him master of Greece and paved the way for the League of Corinth, uniting the Greek world under Macedonian leadership. It was Philip—not Alexander—who laid the foundations for the empire that would soon shake Persia and the ancient world.

This is the story of the king who conquered Greece, reshaped ancient warfare, and prepared the path for one of history’s greatest empires. If you enjoy epic history, ancient battles, and the rise of legendary rulers, subscribe to Epic History for more powerful history shorts.

snippet.title: Napoleon's Masterstroke: The Battle of Montereau
snippet.description:
February 18, 1814. Napoleon Bonaparte had his back against the wall — and he was about to remind Europe exactly why they feared him.

The Coalition armies were closing in on Paris, outnumbering the French at every turn. Most generals would have retreated. Napoleon attacked. At Montereau, on the banks of the Seine and Yonne rivers, he personally seized command of the artillery, reportedly declaring "a battery commander doesn't die — he fights!" and directed his guns with the intensity of a man who had everything to lose.

snippet.title: Saving the Planet with Geo-Engineering | planet:e | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Climate change can be stopped!

Scientists are researching new technical methods to cool the climate. This can only be seen as an emergency rescue plan. These special methods are called geo- or climate-engineering, for example when a lot of chemicals are scattered into the sky to deflect sun rays. But are the risks of these experiments calculable?

snippet.title: Was Alexander The Great Murdered?
snippet.description:
He conquered the known world before the age of 32 — then died in ten days. No wound, no battle, no worthy enemy. Just a banquet, a fever, and silence.

In 323 BC, Alexander the Great collapsed at the palace of Nebuchadnezzar II in Babylon. Within days, the mightiest conqueror the world had ever seen was gone. But here's where history gets dark — his body reportedly showed no signs of decomposition for six days. Was he already dead, or had he been buried alive?

The theories are as compelling as the man himself. Poison — perhaps administered by the regent Antipater — sits at the top of the list. The symptoms match strychnine poisoning almost perfectly. Others point to typhoid fever complicated by bowel perforation, or a lethal amount of wine consumed at Medius of Larissa's infamous feast. A few historians even argue he was struck down by grief following the death of his closest companion, Hephaestion.

But the death itself was only the beginning of the chaos. Alexander left no clear heir and no succession plan. When asked who should inherit his empire, he reportedly whispered "the strongest." Those two words unleashed 40 years of brutal civil war — the Wars of the Diadochi — as his generals tore the greatest empire the ancient world had ever seen into bloody pieces.

The empire that took a genius a lifetime to build was gone within a generation. The mystery of how he died may never be solved — but the world it created, and the world it destroyed, echoes through history to this day.
#AlexanderTheGreat #AncientHistory #epichistory

snippet.title: How Hitler used Fake Sex Scandals to get rid of his Generals
snippet.description:
They never saw it coming — and by the time they did, it was already over.

In February 1938, Adolf Hitler executed one of the most ruthless political purges in modern history — and he didn't fire a single shot to do it. Instead, he used dirt, deception, and manufactured scandal to destroy the very men standing between him and total control of Germany's military.

First came Field Marshal Werner von Blomberg, Germany's War Minister. He had just married a younger woman — but the Gestapo conveniently produced evidence that his new wife had a criminal past. Blomberg was forced to resign in disgrace, shattered and humiliated.

Then came General Werner von Fritsch, Commander-in-Chief of the Army and one of the most respected soldiers in Germany. Hitler's SS fabricated evidence accusing him of homosexuality — a devastating charge in 1930s Germany. Fritsch was hauled before a court, his reputation in ruins. He was later cleared, but it was too late. The damage was done.

Foreign Minister Konstantin von Neurath, seen as too cautious and too conservative for Hitler's aggressive ambitions, was quietly pushed aside and replaced with the fanatically loyal Joachim von Ribbentrop.

With these three men gone, Hitler abolished the War Ministry entirely, created the Oberkommando der Wehrmacht — the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces — and placed himself directly in charge. Sixteen senior generals were dismissed. Dozens more were reassigned.

In a single weekend, Hitler had seized absolute control of the German military machine. No resistance. No rebellion. Just silence.

Within months, he would march into Austria. Within a year, Czechoslovakia. Within two years, the world was at war.

The Blomberg-Fritsch Affair didn't just end three careers — it removed the last internal brake on Adolf Hitler. And the world paid the price.

Would you have seen through the deception — or would you have believed it too? 👇
